q: The total factory overheads of a plant are Rs 6,00,000 and the total direct labour hours are 1,00,000, giving a single blanket rate of Rs 6 per labour hour. A job takes 40 labour hours in Department A, where the departmental rate is Rs 8 per hour, and 30 labour hours in Department B, where the departmental rate is Rs 4 per hour. Compared with the blanket rate, the overhead charged to the job under departmental rates will be:

options.A: Rs 20 less
options.B: The same in both cases
options.C: Rs 20 more
options.D: Rs 60 more

e: Blanket rate charge = (40 + 30) hours x Rs 6 = Rs 420. Departmental charge = 40 x 8 + 30 x 4 = 320 + 120 = Rs 440. The departmental charge is therefore Rs 20 more.

q: A production account, as a form of presenting the cost of production, is distinguished by the fact that it:

options.A: Presents the cost of production in the form of a double-entry account, showing the total cost as well as the cost per unit of output
options.B: Shows only the estimated cost of a job for the purpose of preparing a quotation
options.C: Records only the direct material and direct labour cost of production
options.D: Is prepared only by concerns which render services and do not manufacture goods

e: A production account presents cost of production in double-entry account form and shows both the total cost and the cost per unit of output for the period.

q: The budgeted number of working days of a factory for a month is 25 days. Owing to holidays declared during the month, the factory actually worked for 23 days. The calendar ratio of the factory for the month is:

options.A: 108.70 per cent
options.B: 92 per cent
options.C: 84 per cent
options.D: 100 per cent

e: Calendar ratio = actual working days / budgeted working days x 100 = 23/25 x 100 = 92 per cent.

q: In the scattergraph method of splitting a semi-variable cost into its fixed and variable components:

options.A: The costs of the highest and lowest months only are compared with each other
options.B: A mathematical line is fitted to the cost data by solving simultaneous equations
options.C: Every ledger account is examined one by one and classified as fixed or variable by judgement
options.D: The cost data for a number of periods are plotted on a graph against the level of activity and a line of best fit is drawn by visual inspection

e: In the scattergraph method, costs for a number of periods are plotted against activity levels and a line of best fit is drawn by visual inspection to split the semi-variable cost into fixed and variable parts.

q: The efficiency ratio of a department for a period is 120 per cent and its capacity ratio for the same period is 80 per cent. The activity ratio of the department is:

options.A: 96 per cent
options.B: 200 per cent
options.C: 40 per cent
options.D: 150 per cent

e: Activity ratio = efficiency ratio x capacity ratio = 120% x 80% = 96 per cent.

q: Consider the following statements: 1. The theoretical (maximum) capacity of a plant is the capacity that could be achieved if the plant worked continuously at full efficiency, without any interruption whatsoever. 2. The practical capacity is lower than the theoretical capacity because it makes allowance for unavoidable interruptions such as repairs, maintenance, set-ups and holidays. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both statements are correct: theoretical capacity assumes continuous working at full efficiency with no interruption, while practical capacity is lower because it allows for unavoidable interruptions such as repairs, maintenance, set-ups and holidays.

q: In a factory, 200 units of a product are found to be defective. The cost of production of each unit is Rs 150. The defective units are rectified at an additional cost of Rs 40 per unit and are then sold as seconds for Rs 120 per unit. The net loss arising on the defective units is:
e: Total cost of defective units = production 200 x 150 = 30,000 plus rectification 200 x 40 = 8,000, total 38,000. Sale as seconds realises 200 x 120 = 24,000, so net loss = 38,000 - 24,000 = Rs 14,000.

q: The deprival value (value to the business) of an asset is measured as:

options.A: The higher of its replacement cost and its recoverable amount
options.B: The lower of its replacement cost and its recoverable amount, the recoverable amount being the higher of the value in use and the net selling price
options.C: Its historical cost less the depreciation charged on it up to date
options.D: Its current replacement cost in every case, regardless of the amount recoverable from it

e: Deprival value is the lower of replacement cost and recoverable amount, where recoverable amount is the higher of value in use and net selling price; it is the loss the business would suffer if deprived of the asset.

q: A machine was purchased for Rs 8,00,000. Depreciation is charged at 10 per cent per annum on the written down value. The depreciation charge for the third year is:
e: Written down value method at 10%: year 1 depreciation 80,000, WDV 7,20,000; year 2 depreciation 72,000, WDV 6,48,000; year 3 depreciation = 10% x 6,48,000 = Rs 64,800.

q: Consider the following statements: 1. Dormant stock consists of items of stores which have not been issued or used for a long time but which may still be required at some future date. 2. Obsolete stock consists of items which have become unusable, and are not expected to be used, because of a change in the design, technology or process of production. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: Both 1 and 2
options.B: 1 only
options.C: 2 only
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both statements are correct: dormant stock has not been used for a long time but may still be required in future, while obsolete stock has become unusable and is not expected to be used because of changes in design, technology or process.

q: A plant costs Rs 7,50,000 and has an estimated scrap value of Rs 1,50,000 and an effective life of 5 years. Depreciation is charged by the sum-of-the-years'-digits method. The depreciation charge for the first year is:
e: Depreciable amount = 7,50,000 - 1,50,000 = Rs 6,00,000. Sum of years digits for 5 years = 5+4+3+2+1 = 15. First year depreciation = 5/15 x 6,00,000 = Rs 2,00,000.

q: A quality circle in an organisation is:

options.A: A team of inspectors appointed by management to check the output of each department
options.B: A small group of employees doing similar work who meet voluntarily and regularly to identify, analyse and solve work-related and quality problems in their own area
options.C: A committee of senior managers which fixes the quality standards for the products of the firm
options.D: A group of customers invited periodically to give their opinion on the quality of the products

e: A quality circle is a small group of employees doing similar work who meet voluntarily and regularly to identify, analyse and solve work-related and quality problems in their own area.

q: The profit of a factory under absorption costing exceeds its profit under marginal costing for a period by Rs 18,000. Fixed factory overheads are absorbed at Rs 9 per unit. This shows that during the period:

options.A: The stock of finished goods increased by 2,000 units
options.B: The stock of finished goods decreased by 2,000 units
options.C: The stock of finished goods increased by 1,62,000 units
options.D: There was no change in the stock of finished goods

e: Absorption profit exceeds marginal profit when stock rises, by the fixed overhead carried in the extra stock: increase in finished goods stock = 18,000 / Rs 9 per unit = 2,000 units.

q: The quality trilogy propounded by J. M. Juran consists of the three managerial processes of:

options.A: Quality inspection, quality assurance and quality audit
options.B: Prevention, appraisal and failure analysis
options.C: Quality planning, quality control and quality improvement
options.D: Quality design, quality production and quality marketing

e: Juran's quality trilogy consists of quality planning, quality control and quality improvement, the three managerial processes for managing quality.

q: The profit as per the financial accounts of an enterprise is Rs 2,80,000. The following items are then noticed: dividend received, recorded only in the financial books, Rs 18,000; income tax provided, recorded only in the financial books, Rs 45,000; loss on sale of machinery, recorded only in the financial books, Rs 12,000; notional interest on own capital, charged only in the cost accounts, Rs 20,000; and factory overheads under-absorbed in the cost accounts, Rs 9,000. The profit as per the cost accounts is:
e: Cost profit = financial profit 2,80,000 - dividend received 18,000 (financial books only) + income tax 45,000 + loss on sale of machinery 12,000 (both financial books only) - notional interest on own capital 20,000 (cost books only) + under-absorbed factory overheads 9,000 = Rs 3,08,000.

q: In the classification of the costs of quality, the cost of reviewing and testing the design of a new product before it is released for regular production is classified as a:

options.A: Internal failure cost
options.B: External failure cost
options.C: Appraisal cost
options.D: Prevention cost

e: Reviewing and testing a new product's design before release is a prevention cost in the classification used here: it is appraisal-like checking done at the design stage to prevent defects from entering regular production, not a failure cost.

q: A component is produced in batches. The annual demand is 5,000 units, the set-up cost is Rs 100 per batch and the carrying cost is Rs 5 per unit per year. Production takes place at the rate of 6,250 units per year, while the component is consumed at the rate of the annual demand. Using EBQ = sqrt[(2 x annual demand x set-up cost / carrying cost per unit) x (production rate / (production rate - demand rate))], the Economic Batch Quantity is:

options.A: 1,000 units
options.B: 447 units
options.C: 500 units
options.D: 2,236 units

q: A factory which follows a 'just-in-case' approach to inventory, as opposed to the just-in-time approach, is one which:

options.A: Orders material only after an order for the finished product has been received from a customer
options.B: Keeps no stock of any material and depends entirely on daily deliveries by suppliers
options.C: Produces goods only against confirmed orders and never in anticipation of demand
options.D: Deliberately maintains generous stocks of materials as an insurance against shortages and interruptions in supply, accepting the higher carrying cost involved

e: A just-in-case approach deliberately maintains generous stocks as insurance against shortages and supply interruptions, accepting the higher carrying cost; it is the opposite of just-in-time.

q: A component accounts for 40 per cent of the total cost of a product, while the value (worth) of the function it performs is assessed at only 25 per cent of the total worth of the product. The value index of the component is:
e: Value index = value (worth) percentage / cost percentage = 25 / 40 = 0.625. An index below 1 shows the component's cost share exceeds its worth share, marking it for value analysis.

q: The loss suffered on the sale of an old machine is excluded from the cost accounts principally because it is:

options.A: A capital and financial loss, arising from the disposal of an asset, and not a cost of producing the goods of the period
options.B: An item of factory overhead which has already been absorbed in the cost of production
options.C: A selling expense which is recovered through the selling price of the product
options.D: A charge which the cost accounts record in the following accounting period

e: Loss on sale of an old machine is a capital and financial loss arising from disposal of an asset, not a cost of producing the period's goods, so it is excluded from the cost accounts.

q: A firm prepares a quotation by adding a profit of 25 per cent on the total cost. The same profit, expressed as a percentage of the quotation (selling) price, is:

options.A: 25 per cent
options.B: 33.33 per cent
options.C: 12.50 per cent
options.D: 20 per cent

e: Let total cost be 100, profit 25% on cost = 25, so selling price = 125. Profit as percentage of price = 25/125 x 100 = 20 per cent.

q: A flexible manufacturing system (FMS) in a factory is characterised by:

options.A: The use of general-purpose machines, each attended by several workers, arranged according to the process they perform
options.B: Production lines dedicated permanently to the manufacture of one single product
options.C: Computer-controlled machines linked by automated material handling, which can switch from one product to another with very little set-up time or manual intervention
options.D: The manufacture of every component by skilled craftsmen using hand tools and simple machines

e: A flexible manufacturing system uses computer-controlled machines linked by automated material handling, able to switch between products with very little set-up time or manual intervention.

q: The Finished Goods Ledger Control Account of a factory shows an opening balance of Rs 1,40,000. During the period, finished production transferred from work-in-progress amounted to Rs 9,60,000 and the closing stock of finished goods is Rs 1,25,000. The cost of goods sold transferred out of the account during the period is:
e: Cost of goods sold = opening finished goods 1,40,000 + finished production transferred 9,60,000 - closing finished goods 1,25,000 = Rs 9,75,000.

q: 'Poka-yoke', used in quality management and cost control, refers to:

options.A: Simple mistake-proofing devices or techniques which prevent an error from occurring, or make it immediately evident when it does occur
options.B: The statistical technique of plotting quality costs on a control chart
options.C: The practice of inspecting every unit of output at the end of the production line
options.D: A bonus scheme under which workers are paid for every defect-free unit produced

e: Poka-yoke means simple mistake-proofing devices or techniques that prevent an error from occurring, or make it immediately evident when it does occur.

q: Materials are purchased on credit for the factory. In the cost ledger maintained under the non-integral system, this transaction is recorded by:

options.A: Debiting the supplier's personal account and crediting the Stores Ledger Control Account
options.B: Debiting the Stores Ledger Control Account and crediting the General Ledger Adjustment Account
options.C: Debiting the Work-in-Progress Ledger Control Account and crediting the Stores Ledger Control Account
options.D: Making no entry at all, because purchases on credit are recorded only in the financial books

e: Under the non-integral system, materials bought on credit are recorded in the cost ledger by debiting the Stores Ledger Control Account and crediting the General Ledger Adjustment Account, the supplier's personal account being kept only in the financial books.

q: A project is to be executed in phases. It requires capital expenditure of Rs 7,50,000 at the commencement and a further Rs 3,00,000 on completion of the first phase at the end of Year 2. It is expected to yield net cash inflows of Rs 4,00,000 at the end of Year 3 and Rs 5,00,000 at the end of Year 4. The present value factors at 10% are 0.826 for Year 2, 0.751 for Year 3 and 0.683 for Year 4. The Net Present Value of the project is:
Discounting, as used in the appraisal of a project, is most accurately described as:

options.A: The reverse of compounding, bringing a sum receivable or payable in the future back to its worth at the present time
options.B: The process of adding interest to a present sum to find its future value
options.C: The deduction of a cash discount from the price of an asset when it is purchased
options.D: The writing down of the value of an asset each year by way of depreciation

e: Discounting is the reverse of compounding: it brings a sum receivable or payable in the future back to its present worth using a discount rate.

q: A project requires an outlay of Rs 6,00,000. Its operating net cash inflows are Rs 1,80,000 at the end of each year. If the project is abandoned, it can be sold for Rs 3,60,000 at the end of Year 1 or for Rs 2,60,000 at the end of Year 2. Its bail-out payback period is:

options.A: 1 year
options.B: 2 years
options.C: 3.33 years
options.D: The outlay is never recovered within the life considered

e: Bail-out check: at end of year 1, inflows 1,80,000 + sale value 3,60,000 = 5,40,000, less than the 6,00,000 outlay. By end of year 2, inflows 3,60,000 + sale value 2,60,000 = 6,20,000, exceeding the outlay, so the bail-out payback is 2 years.

q: A project is chosen over another simply because its expected (probability-weighted) net present value is the higher of the two, no separate allowance being made for the greater spread of its possible outcomes. The decision rule so applied rests on the assumption that the decision-maker is:

options.A: Risk-averse, preferring a certain sum to a gamble of equal expected value
options.B: Risk-neutral, valuing a gamble at its expected monetary value regardless of its spread
options.C: Risk-seeking, preferring the gamble with the wider spread of outcomes
options.D: Concerned only with the worst outcome that can occur

e: Choosing purely by the higher probability-weighted (expected) NPV, ignoring the spread of outcomes, values a gamble at its expected monetary value, which is the assumption of a risk-neutral decision-maker.

q: Two mutually exclusive projects, a smaller project S and a larger project L, are under consideration. On the incremental cash flows of L over S (the extra outlay and the extra inflows of the larger project), the net present value is (+) Rs 27,000 at a discount rate of 10% and (-) Rs 13,500 at a discount rate of 20%. By interpolation, the internal rate of return on the incremental cash flows is approximately:

The switching values of the main variables of a project have been worked out as: selling price 4%, sales volume 9%, project cost 6% and operating cost 12%. Judged by these values, the variable to whose estimation and movement the project's viability is most sensitive, and which therefore calls for the closest attention, is:

options.A: The selling price
options.B: The sales volume
options.C: The project cost
options.D: The operating cost

e: The switching value is the percentage change in a variable that wipes out NPV; the smallest switching value means the least room for error. Selling price at 4% is the smallest, so viability is most sensitive to selling price.

q: A project has a Net Present Value of (+) Rs 45,000 and the present value of the outlays on it is Rs 7,50,000. The maximum percentage by which the outlays can increase before the Net Present Value of the project is wiped out (its switching value in respect of the outlay) is:
e: Switching value for outlay = NPV / present value of outlays x 100 = 45,000 / 7,50,000 x 100 = 6.0 per cent.

q: In the certainty-equivalent method of project appraisal, the certainty-equivalent coefficient applied to a cash flow that is regarded as completely certain (riskless) will be:

options.A: Zero
options.B: One
options.C: Equal to the discount rate applied to the flow
options.D: Greater than one

e: In the certainty-equivalent method, a completely certain cash flow needs no risk reduction, so its certainty-equivalent coefficient is one; riskier flows get coefficients below one.

q: An annuity of Rs 2,50,000 receivable at the end of each year is valued at Rs 6,21,750 at a discount rate of 10%. At this rate, the cumulative present value (annuity) factors are 1.736 for 2 years, 2.487 for 3 years and 3.170 for 4 years. The number of years for which the annuity will be received is:

options.A: 2 years
options.B: 4 years
options.C: 2.487 years
options.D: 3 years

e: Number of years is found from the annuity factor implied: 6,21,750 / 2,50,000 = 2.487, which is the given cumulative factor for 3 years at 10%, so the annuity runs for 3 years.

q: In the appraisal of a long-lived project in a period of continuing inflation, the depreciation charged on its plant is computed on the historical cost of the plant. One consequence of this for the appraisal is that:

options.A: The tax saving (tax shield) provided by the depreciation is fixed in money terms, so its value in real terms is steadily eroded by inflation
options.B: The tax shield grows in real terms at the rate of inflation
options.C: Inflation has no effect at all on the value of the tax shield
options.D: The depreciation charge itself rises each year with the general price level

e: Depreciation on historical cost gives a tax shield fixed in money terms; with continuing inflation its real value is steadily eroded, even though the nominal deduction stays the same.

q: A project plant is depreciated by Rs 1,20,000 a year for 4 years and the tax rate is 25%. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 4 years at 10% is 3.170. The present value of the depreciation tax shield of the project is:
e: Annual tax shield = depreciation 1,20,000 x tax rate 25% = Rs 30,000. Present value = 30,000 x annuity factor 3.170 = Rs 95,100.

q: Two projects have the same outlay. One has a short life, its cash inflows being concentrated in the first few years; the other has a long life, a large part of its inflows arising in distant years. If the discount rate used in appraisal is raised, other things being equal:

options.A: The Net Present Value of both the projects will be affected to exactly the same extent
options.B: The Net Present Value of the long-lived project will fall by more, because the discounting bears most heavily on its distant inflows
options.C: The Net Present Value of the short-lived project will fall by more, because its inflows come earlier
options.D: The Net Present Value of neither project will change, because the outlay is the same

e: Discounting bears most heavily on distant cash inflows, so raising the discount rate reduces the NPV of the long-lived project, whose inflows arise later, by more than that of the short-lived project.

q: A project requires an outlay of Rs 8,00,000 and is expected to yield net cash inflows of Rs 2,60,000 at the end of each of the next 4 years (cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 4 years at 10% = 3.170). A major overhaul costing Rs 60,000 will be needed at the end of Year 2 (present value factor for Year 2 at 10% = 0.826). The Net Present Value of the project is:

Appraised as an all-equity (unlevered) project, a proposal has a Net Present Value of (-) Rs 40,000. The present value of the interest tax shield on the debt used to finance it is Rs 1,10,000 and the present value of the costs of issuing the securities to raise the finance is Rs 25,000. Its Adjusted Present Value is:
e: Adjusted Present Value = all-equity NPV (-)40,000 + PV of interest tax shield 1,10,000 - PV of issue costs 25,000 = Rs 45,000.

q: Under a sale and leaseback arrangement, an enterprise:

options.A: Sells an asset it owns to a financier or investor and simultaneously takes the same asset back on lease, so that it keeps the use of the asset while releasing the capital locked up in it
options.B: Sells an asset outright and hires a different asset in its place
options.C: Buys an asset and leases it out to another enterprise for the whole of its life
options.D: Leases an asset with an option to buy it at the end of the lease at its market price

e: In sale and leaseback, the enterprise sells an asset it owns to a financier or investor and simultaneously takes the same asset back on lease, keeping its use while releasing the capital locked up in it.

q: Under a hire-purchase arrangement for acquiring a machine, the ownership (property) of the machine passes to the hirer:

options.A: As soon as the agreement is signed and the machine is delivered to him
options.B: When one-half of the hire-purchase price has been paid
options.C: Only when the last instalment of the hire-purchase price has been paid
options.D: At the end of the first year of the agreement, whatever the payments made

e: Under hire purchase, the hirer is only a bailee until the terms are completed; ownership passes only when the last instalment of the hire-purchase price has been paid.

q: An enterprise expects to have Rs 9,00,000 of retained earnings available for investment. Its target capital structure has 60% equity and 40% debt. The break point of its marginal cost of capital schedule, that is, the total amount of fresh capital it can raise before it must issue new equity shares and its marginal cost of capital rises, is:
e: Break point = retained earnings available / equity proportion in target structure = 9,00,000 / 0.60 = Rs 15,00,000 of total fresh capital before new equity must be issued.

q: An enterprise has before it a schedule of its profitable investment opportunities ranked by their rates of return (an investment opportunity schedule) and a marginal cost of capital schedule that rises as more capital is raised. Its optimal capital budget is the amount of investment at which:

options.A: The total net present value of all the available projects, whether positive or negative, is the highest
options.B: The marginal rate of return on investment just equals the marginal cost of capital, investment beyond that point earning less than its cost
options.C: The average cost of capital of the enterprise is at its lowest
options.D: The whole of the retained earnings of the enterprise are exhausted

e: The optimal capital budget is where the marginal return on investment just equals the marginal cost of capital; investing beyond that point earns less than the cost of the capital used.

q: Broadly, the specific costs of the different sources of long-term finance stand in the order (highest cost first):

options.A: Equity share capital, preference share capital, debentures (debt) reckoned after tax
options.B: Debentures (debt) reckoned after tax, preference share capital, equity share capital
options.C: Preference share capital, equity share capital, debentures (debt) reckoned after tax
options.D: Debentures (debt) reckoned after tax, equity share capital, preference share capital

e: Equity is costliest because it bears the highest risk and gets no tax relief, preference capital comes next, and debenture debt reckoned after tax is cheapest, giving the order equity, preference, debt.

q: The cost of retained earnings used in appraising the finance of an enterprise is properly measured by:

options.A: Zero, because the enterprise makes no payment for the use of its own profits
options.B: The rate of interest payable on the debentures of the enterprise
options.C: The return that the shareholders could earn by investing the amount in securities of comparable risk if it were paid out to them as dividend, that is, their opportunity return
options.D: The rate of dividend last declared by the enterprise on its shares

e: Retained earnings cost the return shareholders could earn on securities of comparable risk if the amount were paid out as dividend; it is an opportunity cost, not zero, even though no payment is made by the enterprise.

q: A 12% debenture of face value Rs 1,000 is redeemable at par at the end of 5 years. Investors require a return of 10% on debentures of this risk. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 5 years at 10% is 3.791 and the present value factor for Year 5 at 10% is 0.621. The value of the debenture is:

options.A: Rs 455

e: Value = PV of interest 120 x 3.791 = 454.92 plus PV of redemption 1,000 x 0.621 = 621, total Rs 1,076 approximately. It exceeds par because the 12% coupon beats the 10% required return.

q: The yield to maturity of a debenture is best defined as:

options.A: The coupon (nominal) rate of interest printed on the debenture
options.B: The discount rate which equates the face value of the debenture with the present value of its redemption proceeds alone, ignoring the interest receipts
options.C: The discount rate which equates the market price of the debenture with the present value of its future interest receipts and redemption proceeds, that is, the internal rate of return of the debenture
options.D: The annual interest on the debenture divided by its current market price

e: Yield to maturity is the discount rate that equates the debenture's market price with the present value of its future interest receipts and redemption proceeds, that is, its internal rate of return.

q: The dividend on preference shares differs from the interest on debentures in an important respect for the enterprise, namely that:

options.A: Non-payment of the preference dividend, unlike default in paying debenture interest, is not an act of default that can lead to proceedings for the winding up of the company
options.B: Preference dividend must be paid whether or not the enterprise earns a profit, just like debenture interest
options.C: Preference dividend is a charge against profits, just like debenture interest
options.D: The holders of preference shares can appoint directors on non-payment of dividend for one year

e: Preference dividend is an appropriation payable only out of profits, so non-payment is not an act of default that can lead to winding-up proceedings, unlike default in paying debenture interest, which is a charge.

q: On the five-factor DuPont decomposition, an enterprise has a tax burden ratio of 0.80, an interest burden ratio of 0.75, an operating (EBIT) margin of 12%, a total assets turnover of 1.6 times and an equity multiplier of 2.5. Its Return on Equity is:
e: Five-factor DuPont ROE = tax burden 0.80 x interest burden 0.75 x EBIT margin 12% x assets turnover 1.6 x equity multiplier 2.5 = 0.288, that is 28.8 per cent.

q: The earnings of an enterprise, in relation to the capital recorded in its books, are persistently far higher than those of comparable enterprises, and the value placed by the market on its business is well in excess of the book amount of its capital. The enterprise is in a state of:

options.A: Under-capitalisation
options.B: Over-capitalisation
options.C: Watered capital
options.D: Over-trading

e: When earnings on the book capital are persistently far above those of comparable firms and market value well exceeds book capital, the enterprise is under-capitalised: it is earning an exceptionally high return on a relatively small capital base.

q: The long-term debt of an enterprise is Rs 18,00,000 and its shareholders' funds are Rs 27,00,000. Its debt to capital employed ratio, capital employed being the long-term debt plus the shareholders' funds, is:
e: Capital employed = long-term debt 18,00,000 + shareholders funds 27,00,000 = 45,00,000. Debt to capital employed = 18,00,000 / 45,00,000 = 0.40 : 1.

q: A company issued its shares to the promoters of a business in payment for assets taken over from them, and those assets were valued for the purpose at amounts far above the prices they could fetch if sold. To the extent of this excess, the share capital of the company is an instance of:

options.A: Reserve capital
options.B: Watered capital
options.C: Preference capital
options.D: Redeemable capital

e: Share capital issued against assets deliberately overvalued above what they could fetch if sold is watered capital to the extent of the excess; that part of the capital is not represented by real value.

q: An enterprise reports net sales of Rs 42,00,000 for a year in which it turned its working capital over 3.5 times. The amount of its net working capital is:
e: Working capital turnover = net sales / net working capital, so net working capital = 42,00,000 / 3.5 = Rs 12,00,000.

q: The capital employed turnover ratio of an enterprise is classified as a composite (mixed) ratio because:

options.A: It is computed by taking an average of several other ratios
options.B: It relates an item taken from the profit and loss account (sales) with an item taken from the balance sheet (capital employed)
options.C: It is used both for measuring liquidity and for measuring solvency
options.D: It is computed for a group of enterprises taken together

e: Capital employed turnover is a composite or mixed ratio because it relates sales, a profit and loss account item, to capital employed, a balance sheet item, linking the two statements.

q: An enterprise is taxed at 40%. Its profit after tax for the year is Rs 4,20,000 and the interest payable by it for the year is Rs 1,80,000. The interest coverage ratio of the enterprise is:

options.A: 4.89 times
options.B: 2.33 times
options.C: 3.89 times
options.D: 5.89 times

e: Profit after tax 4,20,000 at a 40% tax rate gives profit before tax = 4,20,000 / 0.60 = 7,00,000. EBIT = 7,00,000 + interest 1,80,000 = 8,80,000. Interest coverage = 8,80,000 / 1,80,000 = 4.89 times.

q: In computing the Debt Service Coverage Ratio of an enterprise, the earnings figure used is the profit after tax increased by the depreciation charged and the interest payable. Depreciation is added back in this computation mainly because:

options.A: Depreciation is not allowed as a deduction for income-tax purposes
options.B: Debt service, including the repayment of principal, has to be met in cash, and depreciation, being a non-cash charge already deducted in arriving at the profit, does not consume cash
options.C: Depreciation increases the book value of the assets of the enterprise
options.D: The lenders require the enterprise to maintain a depreciation fund equal to the debt

e: Depreciation is added back for debt service coverage because it is a non-cash charge already deducted in arriving at profit; debt service, including principal repayment, must be met in cash.

q: The net sales of an enterprise are Rs 30,00,000. Its gross profit ratio is 30% and its operating profit ratio is 18%. Its operating expenses for the year are:
e: Gross profit = 30% x 30,00,000 = Rs 9,00,000. Operating profit = 18% x 30,00,000 = Rs 5,40,000. Operating expenses = 9,00,000 - 5,40,000 = Rs 3,60,000.

q: A company has 2,00,000 equity shares outstanding on 1 April. On 1 January of the same financial year (that is, with three months of the year remaining) it issues 80,000 further equity shares for cash. Its profit available for the equity shareholders for the year is Rs 11,00,000. Its Earnings Per Share for the year, computed on the weighted average number of shares, is:
e: Weighted average shares = 2,00,000 for the full year + 80,000 x 3/12 = 20,000, total 2,20,000 shares. EPS = 11,00,000 / 2,20,000 = Rs 5.00.

q: A company buys back a part of its own equity shares from the market at a price which is below the book value per share of the shares. Other things remaining unchanged, the effect of this buy-back on the book value per share of the shares that remain is that it:

options.A: Rises, because the cash paid out per share bought back is less than the book value attributable to that share
options.B: Falls, because the cash resources of the company are reduced by the buy-back
options.C: Remains unchanged, because the number of shares and the net assets fall in the same proportion
options.D: Falls, because the reserves of the company are reduced by the buy-back

e: Buying back shares below book value per share pays out less cash per share cancelled than the book value attributable to it, so the remaining net assets are spread over the remaining shares at a higher book value per share.

q: The equity share capital of a company is Rs 15,00,000, its reserves and surplus are Rs 9,00,000, it has preference share capital of Rs 4,00,000 and it carries preliminary expenses of Rs 60,000 as an asset. It has 1,50,000 equity shares. The book value per equity share is:
e: Equity shareholders funds = equity capital 15,00,000 + reserves 9,00,000 - preliminary expenses 60,000 = Rs 23,40,000; preference capital is excluded. Book value per equity share = 23,40,000 / 1,50,000 = Rs 15.60.

q: A share carrying a right to a dividend about to be paid is quoted cum-dividend. When the share begins to be quoted ex-dividend, that is, without the right to that dividend passing to the buyer, its market price, other things being equal, will:

options.A: Rise by approximately the amount of the dividend
options.B: Fall by twice the amount of the dividend
options.C: Remain exactly unchanged, because the dividend is paid by the company and not by the seller
options.D: Fall by approximately the amount of the dividend, because the buyer will not receive the dividend that is about to be paid

e: When a share goes ex-dividend the buyer no longer receives the imminent dividend, so, other things equal, its market price falls by approximately the amount of that dividend.

q: The market price of a company's share is Rs 260 cum-rights. The company offers a rights issue of 1 new share for every 4 shares held, at a subscription price of Rs 180 per new share. The value of one right (the entitlement attaching to one existing share) is:

options.A: Rs 80
options.B: Rs 20
options.C: Rs 244
options.D: Rs 16

e: Ex-rights price = (4 x 260 + 1 x 180) / 5 = 1,220 / 5 = Rs 244. Value of one right per existing share = cum-rights price 260 - ex-rights price 244 = Rs 16.

q: The essential purpose of offering a rights issue to the existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings, rather than offering the new shares directly to the public, is:

options.A: To enable the company to issue the shares at a price higher than the market price
options.B: To protect the existing shareholders from the dilution of their proportionate ownership and voting power in the company
options.C: To avoid the payment of underwriting commission on the issue
options.D: To ensure that the issue is fully subscribed in all circumstances

e: A rights issue in proportion to existing holdings protects existing shareholders from dilution of their proportionate ownership and voting power, as each can subscribe pro rata or sell the rights.

q: A company is expected to pay a constant dividend of Rs 14 per share every year indefinitely, with no growth. The cost of equity capital of the company is 16%. The price of its share, on the dividend capitalisation basis, is:
e: With a constant perpetual dividend and no growth, price = dividend / cost of equity = 14 / 0.16 = Rs 87.50.

q: The intrinsic value of a share, as estimated by an investor from the present value of the benefits he expects from it, is Rs 210, while the share is quoted in the market at Rs 175. On this estimate, the correct reading is that the share is:

options.A: Overvalued in the market and should be sold
options.B: Undervalued in the market, its expected benefits being worth more than its price, and is worth buying
options.C: Correctly valued, because the market price is always the intrinsic value
options.D: Undervalued, and its price must immediately rise to Rs 210

e: Intrinsic value Rs 210 exceeds the market price Rs 175, so on the investor's estimate the share is undervalued in the market and is worth buying; this is an estimate, not a guarantee the price must rise at once.

q: In a sub-division (split) of its equity shares, a company reduces the face value of each share from Rs 100 to Rs 20 and increases the number of shares fivefold. The immediate effect of the split is that:

options.A: The total share capital of the company increases fivefold
options.B: The reserves and surplus of the company are capitalised to the extent of the split
options.C: The total share capital and the reserves remain unchanged, only the number of shares and the face value and market price per share changing in inverse proportion
options.D: The book value of the holdings of each shareholder falls to one-fifth

e: In a share split only the denomination changes: face value falls and the number of shares rises in inverse proportion, while total share capital, reserves and each holder's total book value remain unchanged.

q: An enterprise borrows Rs 6,34,000, repayable in 4 equal annual instalments of Rs 2,00,000 each, the instalments covering both interest and repayment of principal. The total interest it pays over the whole term of the loan is:
e: Total paid over the loan = 4 instalments x 2,00,000 = Rs 8,00,000. Amount borrowed was 6,34,000, so total interest = 8,00,000 - 6,34,000 = Rs 1,66,000.

q: In a decision tree drawn for the appraisal of a project, the square nodes and the circle nodes stand, respectively, for:

options.A: Decision points, at which the decision-maker chooses between alternative courses of action, and chance points, at which the outcome depends on events governed by probabilities
options.B: Chance points and decision points, in that order
options.C: Points at which cash inflows arise and points at which cash outflows arise
options.D: Points at which the project can be abandoned and points at which it must be continued

e: In a decision tree, square nodes are decision points where the decision-maker chooses between alternatives, and circle nodes are chance points where the outcome depends on events governed by probabilities.

q: The net fixed assets of an enterprise are Rs 21,00,000 and its fixed assets ratio (net fixed assets divided by long-term funds) is 0.75. Its long-term funds are:
e: Fixed assets ratio = net fixed assets / long-term funds, so long-term funds = 21,00,000 / 0.75 = Rs 28,00,000.

q: The chief use of common-size (vertical) statements in the analysis of financial statements is that, by expressing every item as a percentage of a common base, they:

options.A: Remove the effect of the size of the enterprise, so that the structure of its statements can be compared between periods and with enterprises of a different size
options.B: Show the change in each item between two dates in absolute and percentage terms
options.C: Convert the historical costs in the statements into current values
options.D: Enable the exact profit of the enterprise to be forecast for the next year

e: Common-size statements express every item as a percentage of a common base, removing the effect of size, so the structure can be compared between periods and with enterprises of different size.

q: A production department reports a favourable material price variance because cheaper material was bought, but in the same period adverse material usage and labour efficiency variances are reported. In investigating these variances, the sound approach is to:

options.A: Judge the purchase manager's performance solely by the favourable price variance
options.B: Look at the variances together, because they may be interdependent, the saving on price having possibly caused the extra consumption and the loss of efficiency through inferior material
options.C: Ignore the adverse variances, since the net variance is small
options.D: Transfer the adverse variances to the sales department

e: Variances may be interdependent: cheaper but inferior material can cause the favourable price variance and the adverse usage and labour efficiency variances together, so they must be investigated jointly, not department by department in isolation.

q: Under negotiated budgeting, the final budget of a department is arrived at by:

options.A: The top management fixing the figures and merely informing the department of them
options.B: The department fixing its own figures, which the top management must accept without change
options.C: Successive rounds in which proposals come up from the operating levels and targets and comments come down from the higher levels, until an agreed and feasible budget emerges
options.D: Copying the budget of a competing enterprise with suitable changes of name

e: Under negotiated budgeting, proposals come up from operating levels and targets and comments come down from higher levels in successive rounds, until an agreed and feasible budget emerges.

q: The chief weakness of fixing the advertising budget as a percentage of sales is that:

options.A: Advertising is made to follow sales instead of influencing them, so that the amount provided falls when sales fall, which is precisely when advertising support may be needed most
options.B: The percentage cannot be calculated unless the sales are known in advance
options.C: Advertising expenditure can never be expressed as a percentage of anything
options.D: The method is permitted only for the advertising of new products

e: Fixing advertising as a percentage of sales makes advertising follow sales rather than influence them; the provision then falls when sales fall, precisely when advertising support may be needed most.

q: A long-term budget of an enterprise is best described as a budget which:

options.A: Covers the next month in full detail, item by item
options.B: Is prepared only for the cash receipts and payments of the next quarter
options.C: Can never be revised once it has been approved
options.D: Covers a period of several years in broad and strategic terms, laying down the direction of growth and the major programmes, within which the annual budgets are then prepared in detail

e: A long-term budget covers several years in broad, strategic terms, laying down the direction of growth and major programmes, within which detailed annual budgets are then prepared.

q: A department reports an adverse cost variance which is within the range that experience shows to arise from normal random fluctuations in the process. The correct control response is that:

options.A: The manager must be penalised, because every adverse variance is a fault
options.B: Such a chance variance, lying within the accepted tolerance limits, does not by itself call for investigation or blame, attention being reserved for variances that fall outside those limits
options.C: The budget should be revised at once to remove the variance
options.D: The variance should be hidden by adjusting the stock figures

e: A variance within the range of normal random fluctuation lies within accepted tolerance limits and is a chance variance; by itself it calls for no investigation or blame, attention being reserved for variances outside those limits.

q: When the functional budgets of an enterprise have been consolidated, the budgeted balance sheet is expected to tally. If it does not tally, the usual inference is that:

options.A: The sales budget must be increased until the balance sheet tallies
options.B: The enterprise is certain to make a loss in the budget period
options.C: Some budgeted transaction has been omitted or double-counted, or an opening balance has been wrongly carried in, so that the budgets need to be checked for completeness and consistency
options.D: The cash budget should be discarded altogether

e: A budgeted balance sheet that does not tally signals an omission, double-counting or a wrongly carried opening balance somewhere in the functional budgets, which must be checked for completeness and consistency.

q: Experience shows that the single most important condition for a budgetary control system to succeed in practice is:

options.A: Wholehearted support and commitment of the top management, shown by taking the budgets seriously in review and decision-making, and not merely approving them formally
options.B: The purchase of an expensive budgeting software package
options.C: The appointment of the external auditor as the budget officer
options.D: The preparation of the maximum possible number of budget statements

e: The single most important condition for budgetary control to succeed is wholehearted top management support, shown by taking budgets seriously in review and decision-making, not merely approving them formally.

q: The sales department proposes a budget of 1,00,000 units, the production department reports a capacity of only 80,000 units and the finance department reports that cash will not support even that level. The role of the budget committee in such a situation is to:

options.A: Accept all the three proposals as they stand and consolidate them
options.B: Reject the budgets of all the three departments for the whole year
options.C: Leave each department to work to its own figures independently
options.D: Examine the conflicting proposals together, reconcile them by phasing, capacity additions, price or credit changes, and settle one coordinated and feasible plan for the enterprise as a whole

e: The budget committee must examine conflicting departmental proposals together and reconcile them by measures such as phasing, capacity additions, price or credit changes, settling one coordinated and feasible plan for the whole enterprise.

q: Besides the budget calendar and the forms to be used, a budget manual also commonly lays down:

options.A: The selling prices to be charged to each individual customer
options.B: The procedure for obtaining proper approval for expenditure not provided for in the budget, or in excess of the amount provided, so that no manager treats the budget as either rigid or freely exceedable
options.C: The names of the suppliers from whom materials must be bought
options.D: The dividend to be declared by the enterprise at the end of the year

e: A budget manual also commonly lays down the procedure for obtaining proper approval for expenditure not provided for in the budget, or in excess of the amount provided, alongside the budget calendar and forms.

q: Budgetary control reports lose most of their value if they are prepared perfectly but reach the managers long after the period to which they relate. This is because:

options.A: Managers are interested only in the reports of the current month
options.B: Reports are required to be filed with the auditors before they are seen by managers
options.C: Control is exercised by acting on deviations, and action can be effective only while the period is still current or recent, so reports should be prompt, even if they are based on reasonably approximate figures
options.D: Late reports are not accepted as evidence in any proceeding

e: Control works by acting on deviations, and action is effective only while the period is current or recent; budgetary control reports must therefore be prompt, even if based on reasonably approximate figures.

q: Budgeted sales of a product are 68,000 units. The opening stock of finished goods is 8,000 units and the closing stock is to be raised to 12,000 units. Experience shows that 10% of the units started in production are rejected as defective and yield no good output. The number of units to be started in production is:

options.A: 80,000 units
options.B: 72,000 units
options.C: 79,200 units
options.D: 68,000 units

e: Good units needed = budgeted sales 68,000 + closing stock 12,000 - opening stock 8,000 = 72,000. With 10% rejected, units to be started = 72,000 / 0.90 = 80,000 units.

q: The total market demand for a product in the current year is 5,00,000 units and it is expected to grow by 20% in the budget year. The enterprise expects to secure a 20% share of the total market in the budget year and to sell its product at Rs 50 per unit. Its budgeted sales value for the budget year is:
e: Budget year market = 5,00,000 x 1.20 = 6,00,000 units. Enterprise share 20% = 1,20,000 units, at Rs 50 = Rs 60,00,000 budgeted sales value.

q: An enterprise budgets to sell 50,000 units at Rs 80 per unit. Sales returns are expected to be 2% of the units sold, and a trade discount of 5% is allowed on the invoice price of the goods actually retained by the customers. The budgeted net sales value is:
e: Gross sales = 50,000 x 80 = Rs 40,00,000. Returns 2% leave 49,000 units retained, invoiced at 49,000 x 80 = 39,20,000. Trade discount 5% = 1,96,000, so net sales = 39,20,000 - 1,96,000 = Rs 37,24,000.

q: The budgeted sales value of an enterprise for a period is Rs 18,00,000. Its budgeted cost of production is Rs 12,00,000, it also buys finished goods for resale for Rs 1,00,000, and its stock of finished goods is valued at Rs 1,80,000 at the commencement of the period and Rs 2,20,000 at the end of the period. Its budgeted gross profit for the period is:
e: Cost of goods sold = cost of production 12,00,000 + finished goods bought 1,00,000 + opening stock 1,80,000 - closing stock 2,20,000 = 12,60,000. Budgeted gross profit = sales 18,00,000 - 12,60,000 = Rs 5,40,000.

q: An enterprise purchases materials on terms that 40% of each month's purchases are paid in the month of purchase, a cash discount of 2% being earned on such payments, and the balance is paid in the following month. Its purchases were Rs 4,00,000 in March and are budgeted at Rs 5,00,000 in April. The cash to be paid to creditors in April is:
e: April payments: March balance paid in April = 60% x 4,00,000 = 2,40,000. April purchases paid in April = 40% x 5,00,000 = 2,00,000 less 2% discount 4,000 = 1,96,000. Total cash to creditors = 2,40,000 + 1,96,000 = Rs 4,36,000.

q: Under a pledge of goods as security for a bank advance for working capital:

options.A: The goods remain in the godown of the borrower and the bank has no right over them
options.B: The ownership of the goods passes permanently to the bank
options.C: The goods are delivered into the possession of the bank, or of its godown-keeper, as security, the ownership remaining with the borrower, and the goods are released as the advance is repaid
options.D: The bank advances the money only against the personal guarantee of the borrower

e: Under a pledge, the goods are delivered into the possession of the bank or its godown-keeper as security, ownership remaining with the borrower, and the goods are released as the advance is repaid.

q: A floating charge created over the current assets of an enterprise has the distinctive feature that:

options.A: It hovers over a shifting body of assets, such as stock and book debts, and the enterprise remains free to deal with those assets in the ordinary course of business until the charge crystallises into a fixed charge on the happening of a specified event, such as default
options.B: It is a charge that carries a floating rate of interest in every case
options.C: It prevents the enterprise from selling any of its stock until the loan is fully repaid
options.D: It can be created only over the cash balance of the enterprise

e: A floating charge hovers over a shifting body of assets such as stock and book debts, leaving the enterprise free to deal with them in the ordinary course of business until the charge crystallises into a fixed charge on a specified event such as default.

q: A customer discounts the bills receivable of his enterprise with his bank and receives the proceeds. Until the bills mature and are honoured, the position is that:

options.A: The bank can never claim anything from the customer in respect of the bills
options.B: The bills cease to be connected with the enterprise in any way
options.C: The enterprise need not disclose anything about the discounted bills in its accounts
options.D: The bank retains recourse to the enterprise, so that if a bill is dishonoured on maturity the bank can recover the amount from the enterprise, the discounted bills being in the nature of a contingent liability until they are met

e: When bills are discounted, the bank retains recourse to the enterprise: if a bill is dishonoured at maturity the bank can recover from the enterprise, so discounted bills are a contingent liability until they are met.

q: An enterprise is required to keep margin money in a deposit with its bank as a condition of the bank issuing guarantees and letters of credit on its behalf. The effect of this requirement on its working capital is that:

options.A: It reduces the working capital requirement, because the guarantees replace cash in every respect
options.B: A part of its funds stands blocked in the deposit and is not available for meeting its operating needs, so that the working capital it must arrange for its operations is increased to that extent
options.C: It has no effect at all, because margin money is not an asset of the enterprise
options.D: The margin money is treated as a part of the share capital of the enterprise

e: Margin money for guarantees and letters of credit stands blocked in a deposit with the bank and is not available for operating needs, so the working capital the enterprise must arrange for operations increases to that extent.

q: Under a usance bill drawn on 'documents against acceptance' terms in trade finance:

options.A: The shipping documents are handed to the buyer only after he has paid the full amount of the bill in cash
options.B: No bill of exchange is drawn at all in such a transaction
options.C: The shipping documents are released to the buyer when he accepts the bill, that is, undertakes to pay it, and the payment itself is made on the due date at the end of the usance or credit period
options.D: The bank guarantees that the buyer will never default on the bill

e: On documents against acceptance terms, the shipping documents are released to the buyer when he accepts the bill, undertaking to pay it; payment itself is made on the due date at the end of the usance period.

q: Under a supplier-finance (reverse factoring) arrangement for working capital:

options.A: The buyer confirms the invoices of its suppliers to a bank or finance platform, the financier pays the suppliers early, and the buyer pays the financier on the original due date, so that the suppliers get prompt payment while the buyer retains its normal credit period
options.B: The suppliers of an enterprise are required to lend money to the enterprise for a year
options.C: The enterprise sells its fixed assets to its suppliers and leases them back
options.D: The bank pays the buyer instead of paying the suppliers of the buyer

e: In supplier finance or reverse factoring, the buyer confirms suppliers invoices to a financier, who pays the suppliers early, while the buyer pays the financier on the original due date, retaining its normal credit period.

q: Interest on a cash credit account for working capital is charged by the bank:

options.A: On the whole of the limit sanctioned, whether it is drawn or not
options.B: Only on the days on which the borrower visits the bank
options.C: At a fixed amount agreed at the time of sanction, regardless of the drawings
options.D: On the amount actually outstanding in the account from day to day, that is, on the daily balances drawn, and not on the sanctioned limit as such

e: Interest on a cash credit account is charged on the amount actually outstanding day to day, that is on the daily balances drawn, not on the whole sanctioned limit.

q: Banks periodically arrange a stock audit of a borrower enjoying working capital limits mainly in order to:

options.A: Prepare the annual accounts of the borrower on his behalf
options.B: Verify the existence, quantity, condition and valuation of the stocks charged to the bank and the correctness of the stock statements on the basis of which drawing power is allowed
options.C: Fix the selling prices of the products of the borrower
options.D: Decide the dividend to be paid by the borrower

e: A bank's stock audit verifies the existence, quantity, condition and valuation of stocks charged to it and the correctness of the stock statements on which drawing power is allowed.

q: An enterprise follows a restrictive policy in holding current assets, keeping its stock and debtors at a low level in relation to its sales. The expected consequence of this policy is that:

options.A: Its return will necessarily be low and its risk also low
options.B: Its working capital will be the highest in its industry
options.C: Profitability may be higher because less funds remain locked up in current assets, but the risk of stock-outs, interrupted production and lost sales through tight credit is also higher
options.D: It will never face any risk of a shortage of stock

e: A restrictive current asset policy locks up less funds, which may raise profitability, but it raises risk: low stock and tight credit to customers can cause stock-outs, interrupted production and lost sales.

q: A revolving line of credit sanctioned by a bank to an enterprise differs from an ordinary term loan mainly in that:

options.A: Within the sanctioned limit and during the period of the agreement, the enterprise may draw, repay and draw again repeatedly, instead of receiving the whole amount once and repaying it only in fixed instalments
options.B: No interest is charged on the amounts drawn under a line of credit
options.C: A line of credit can be used only for purchasing fixed assets
options.D: The bank can never withdraw a line of credit under any circumstances

e: A revolving line of credit lets the enterprise draw, repay and draw again repeatedly within the sanctioned limit during the agreement period, unlike a term loan received once and repaid in fixed instalments.

q: An enterprise takes a credit insurance cover on its trade receivables. The main protection such a cover gives to its working capital is against:

options.A: A fall in the market price of its finished goods
options.B: Damage to its stock by fire and flood
options.C: Fraud committed by its own employees in the cash office
options.D: Loss arising from the failure or insolvency of its buyers to pay for the goods supplied to them on credit, so that a bad debt does not suddenly drain its working capital

e: Credit insurance on trade receivables protects working capital against loss from buyers failing or becoming insolvent and not paying for goods supplied on credit, so a bad debt does not suddenly drain working capital.

q: A bank has sanctioned a cash credit limit of Rs 10,00,000 to an enterprise. The paid-for stock of the enterprise is Rs 8,00,000, on which a margin of 25% is prescribed, and its book debts outstanding for not more than 90 days are Rs 4,00,000, on which a margin of 40% is prescribed. It also has book debts of Rs 1,00,000 outstanding for more than 90 days, which are not eligible, and stock of Rs 2,00,000 which has not been paid for, which is also not eligible. The maximum amount the enterprise can actually draw is:
e: Drawing power: paid-for stock 8,00,000 less 25% margin = 6,00,000, plus book debts up to 90 days 4,00,000 less 40% margin = 2,40,000, total Rs 8,40,000. Debts over 90 days and unpaid stock are ineligible, and 8,40,000 is below the 10,00,000 limit, so maximum drawing is Rs 8,40,000.

q: An enterprise is considering offering a cash discount of 2% to its credit customers. Its credit sales are Rs 30,00,000 a year and 50% of the customers are expected to avail of the discount. The average receivables will fall from Rs 5,00,000 to Rs 2,50,000, and the cost of capital of the enterprise is 15% per annum. The net effect of the proposal is:

options.A: A net loss of Rs 30,000
options.B: A net gain of Rs 37,500
options.C: A net gain of Rs 7,500
options.D: A net loss of Rs 7,500

e: Discount cost = 2% x 50% x 30,00,000 = Rs 30,000. Saving in cost of capital = receivables reduction (5,00,000 - 2,50,000) x 15% = Rs 37,500. Net effect = 37,500 - 30,000 = a net gain of Rs 7,500.

q: A bank lends Rs 5,00,000 to an enterprise for one year at 10% per annum, the interest for the year being deducted in advance at the time the loan is granted, so that the enterprise actually receives the balance. The effective rate of interest borne by the enterprise on the funds it actually receives is:
e: Interest for the year = 10% x 5,00,000 = Rs 50,000, deducted in advance, so the enterprise actually receives 4,50,000. Effective rate = 50,000 / 4,50,000 x 100 = 11.11 per cent.

q: The sales of an enterprise are expected to rise by 25%. At the present level of sales, its current assets are Rs 9,00,000, which include a cash balance of Rs 1,00,000 that will remain unchanged, the other current assets varying in proportion to sales, and its current liabilities are Rs 4,00,000, varying in proportion to sales. The additional working capital it will require is:
e: Variable current assets = 9,00,000 - fixed cash 1,00,000 = 8,00,000, rising 25% by 2,00,000. Current liabilities 4,00,000 rise 25% by 1,00,000, financing part of the increase. Additional working capital = 2,00,000 - 1,00,000 = Rs 1,00,000.
